claims.title: Unauthenticated firmware polling can exhaust public bucket capacity or delivery budget
claims.description: Any internet attacker can repeatedly request firmware through the public-read `flow:sensor-node-to-firmware-bucket:poll-firmware` path against `store:firmware-bucket`, consuming object-read throughput, egress quota, or metered delivery budget at far less cost than serving firmware images. If the bucket has no request-rate, bandwidth, or budget limits for anonymous readers, this can throttle or exhaust capacity needed by legitimate `entity:sensor-node` firmware polls. Second-order, a prolonged outage or throttling of firmware delivery prevents the fleet from retrieving updates; the affected nodes are tagged `availability-critical`, so an attacker can impede maintenance of deployed devices without needing to compromise a node.

grounds.text: The bucket is public read, because making the nodes authenticate to it was awkward.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high because `flow:sensor-node-to-firmware-bucket:poll-firmware` permits unauthenticated public reads from anywhere; impact is high because exhaustion that blocks firmware delivery affects `entity:sensor-node`, which is tagged `availability-critical`.

mitigations.summary: Require a bounded device identity for firmware retrieval
mitigations.detail: Replace anonymous access on `flow:sensor-node-to-firmware-bucket:poll-firmware` with short-lived, device-bound credentials or signed download requests, enabling per-device revocation and quota enforcement.

mitigations.summary: Limit anonymous-delivery resource consumption until authentication is deployed
mitigations.detail: Configure request, concurrency, bandwidth, and egress-budget limits for `store:firmware-bucket`, with alerting on anomalous read rates, so excessive polling is rejected before it consumes firmware-delivery capacity.

mitigations.summary: Make firmware retrieval resilient to temporary delivery pressure
mitigations.detail: Use bounded retries with backoff and jitter in `entity:sensor-node` polling behavior so a bucket slowdown does not create a synchronized retry storm across the fleet.

claims.title: A shared fleet key lets a compromised node authenticate as any sensor
claims.description: An attacker who obtains the fleet-wide pre-shared key can present it on `flow:sensor-node-to-device-gateway:publish-readings` to `process:device-gateway` and be accepted as an apparently legitimate `entity:sensor-node`, rather than as the specific node from which the key was obtained. The key is shared by every device and is never rotated, so the gateway cannot distinguish the impostor from any genuine fleet member. Second-order: accepted readings traverse `flow:device-gateway-to-telemetry-normalizer:forward-readings` and are loaded into `store:telemetry-lake`, allowing the attacker to establish a durable false sensor identity capable of submitting fleet telemetry at platform scale.

grounds.text: The key is per fleet, not per device. Nobody has rotated it since deployment.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high because `flow:sensor-node-to-device-gateway:publish-readings` crosses from the field network to the internet-facing `process:device-gateway`, while the submitted description states that one unrotated key is shared across every device. Impact is high because the impersonated device can submit accepted readings that reach `store:telemetry-lake`, which is tagged `pii` and `business-critical-data`, across a fleet of thousands of nodes rather than one device.

mitigations.summary: Issue a unique, revocable identity to every sensor node
mitigations.detail: Replace the fleet-wide pre-shared key on `flow:sensor-node-to-device-gateway:publish-readings` with per-device certificates or workload credentials bound to a device identifier and customer assignment.

mitigations.summary: Rotate and scope existing fleet credentials during migration
mitigations.detail: Until per-device identity is deployed, rotate the shared key, limit its accepted scope, and monitor `process:device-gateway` for simultaneous or anomalous device identities.

claims.title: Fleet-key holder can flood the device gateway and propagate ingest overload
claims.description: An attacker who obtains the fleet-wide pre-shared key from one deployed `entity:sensor-node` can send high-rate MQTT publishes over `flow:sensor-node-to-device-gateway:publish-readings` to `process:device-gateway`. Each accepted publish drives a device-registry lookup over `flow:device-gateway-to-device-registry:look-up-device` and forwarding over `flow:device-gateway-to-telemetry-normalizer:forward-readings`; this makes the attacker’s message-generation cost lower than the broker, registry, and downstream processing cost. If per-device quotas, connection limits, and load shedding are not configured, the attacker can exhaust broker connections, worker capacity, or downstream throughput and deny legitimate fleet telemetry. Second-order, overload crosses into `boundary:analytics-core`, delaying `process:telemetry-normalizer` and its writes to `store:telemetry-lake`, so dashboards and telemetry ingestion are impaired for other customers as well.

claims.title: An unverified gateway-to-core publisher boundary may let an ingress foothold obtain analytics ingestion authority
claims.description: `process:device-gateway` is internet-facing and publishes accepted readings across `crossing:flow:device-gateway-to-telemetry-normalizer:forward-readings` from the ingest edge into the analytics core, but authentication on that flow is unknown. If that Pub/Sub path does not authenticate and restrict publishers to the intended gateway workload, an attacker who obtains a foothold in the exposed gateway can publish work as an internal producer to `process:telemetry-normalizer`. The attacker thereby moves from ingress-edge access into analytics ingestion authority, beyond the authority of an external node. Second-order, the normalizer writes those messages into `store:telemetry-lake` through `flow:telemetry-normalizer-to-telemetry-lake:load-readings`, so forged producer input can be committed through the ordinary analytics path. This threat is conditional on resolving the unknown authentication state of the gateway-to-normalizer flow.

claims.title: Fleet-wide key prevents attribution of disputed sensor readings to a device
claims.description: Any holder of the fleet-wide credential can publish a reading on `flow:sensor-node-to-device-gateway:publish-readings` to `process:device-gateway` across the field-to-ingest trust boundary. Because the credential is shared by every `entity:sensor-node` rather than bound to one device, even a retained record can establish only that some fleet-key holder acted, not which node produced a disputed reading. A customer can therefore deny that a reading attributed to its site was emitted by its node. The accepted readings continue through `flow:device-gateway-to-telemetry-normalizer:forward-readings` and `flow:telemetry-normalizer-to-telemetry-lake:load-readings`, so this attribution gap undermines the evidential value of historical readings in `store:telemetry-lake`, including site addresses and occupancy patterns.

rejected_claims.title: A fleet-wide device key can grant a node another device's ingestion authority
rejected_claims.description: A holder of the pre-shared key used on `flow:sensor-node-to-device-gateway:publish-readings` can present a different device identifier to `process:device-gateway`. The key is explicitly per fleet rather than per device, while the gateway uses the device lookup to determine the customer assignment. If the registry lookup does not additionally bind the presented identifier to a distinct device-specific identity, a node or key holder can cause the gateway to accept readings as another device and gain that device's ingestion authority. This is horizontal escalation through `process:device-gateway`, rather than merely authentication as a fleet member. Second-order, accepted readings traverse `flow:device-gateway-to-telemetry-normalizer:forward-readings` and are loaded into the telemetry lake, allowing falsified readings to enter the normal customer-data pipeline.
